name: Design a Container Registry
intent: Store and serve container images by content hash, so that identical layers are kept once, pushes can resume, pulls are fast in every region, and old data is deleted without breaking a push in progress.
codeTitle: a content-addressed registry with resumable uploads and safe garbage collection
finalIntro: One image pushed by a build, scanned, and pulled by a server in another region.
prompt: Design a private container registry for a company with thousands of engineers and tens of thousands of servers. Builds push images, servers pull them, and the registry keeps every image that is in use. Pushes of several gigabytes must survive a dropped connection, pulls must be fast in every region, unused data must be cleaned up, and the company wants to know that what runs in production was built by its own pipeline and has no known vulnerabilities.
functional: Push an image made of layers and a manifest, and tag it
Pull an image by tag or by its digest
Keep layers that several images share only once
Pull through a cache of a public registry, and copy images to other regions
Delete untagged images and unreferenced layers on a schedule
Scan images for known vulnerabilities and verify signatures
nonFunctional: A layer is always returned exactly as it was pushed, and every pull verifies its hash
Pulling an image that a region already holds takes under a second to start and runs at network speed
Handle thousands of pulls per second at the peak, for layers of hundreds of megabytes
Never delete a layer that a manifest, or a push in progress, still needs
Pulls keep working when the public upstream registry is slow or rate-limiting us
Storage cost grows with new bytes, not with the number of images
Production can refuse images that are unsigned or that have critical vulnerabilities

firstAttempt.text: One web server with a disk. An image is a folder named by repository and tag. A push uploads the whole image as one request and overwrites the folder, and a pull downloads the whole folder.
limits: Two images that share the same 200 MB base layer each store their own copy of it
A connection that drops at 90% of a 2 GB push starts again from zero
Pushing the tag 'latest' again silently replaces the image, and nobody can say exactly what was running yesterday
All pulls come through the one server, which runs out of bandwidth when a thousand nodes deploy together
Deleting old folders is only safe if nobody is using them, and nothing says whether they are in use
Nothing proves that the bytes pulled are the bytes that were pushed, or who built them

steps.title: Name every blob by the hash of its bytes
steps.problem: Folders named by repository and tag copy shared data over and over, let a tag be overwritten without a trace, and give no way to check that the bytes are the ones that were pushed.
steps.fix: Store every layer and every config as a blob whose name is its digest, the hash of its content, such as sha256:9f86d0... The same bytes always have the same name, so a layer shared by a thousand images is stored once. A manifest is a small document that lists the digests of the config and of the layers, and the manifest has its own digest too. A tag such as 'app:v7' is only a mutable pointer in a metadata database from a name to a manifest digest. Pulling by tag asks 'what does v7 point at now?', and pulling by digest asks for exactly one immutable thing. Every client recomputes the hash of what it received, so corruption and tampering are detected.
steps.tradeoff: Storage grows with the new bytes, history is exact, and pulls can be verified end to end. A digest is useless to read, so people still need tags, and tags can move: deployments should record the digest that a tag resolved to. Hash computation costs some CPU on every upload.

steps.title: Upload in resumable chunks, and serve blobs by redirect
steps.problem: A 2 GB layer pushed in one request fails in the last seconds, and every pull passing through the API servers makes them a bandwidth bottleneck.
steps.fix: A push starts with a HEAD request per layer (a cheap check of whether the registry has it), and layers the registry already has are skipped. For a missing layer the client opens an upload session and sends chunks, each at an explicit offset. The server accepts a chunk only at the offset it expects, and after a failure the client asks where the upload stands and continues from there. The final request names the digest, the server recomputes the hash of everything received, and only then publishes the blob. Pulls answer with a redirect to a signed, expiring URL on the CDN or the blob store, so the heavy bytes never go through the API.
steps.tradeoff: Large pushes survive bad networks and bandwidth scales with the blob store and the CDN. Upload sessions are state that needs expiry, since abandoned sessions hold space, and the registry must verify the digest at the end because it cannot trust the client's claim.

steps.title: Put a pull-through cache in front of public registries
steps.problem: Builds and nodes pull base images such as ubuntu from a public registry, which rate-limits anonymous pulls and sometimes goes down, and that breaks deployments for reasons nobody here controls.
steps.fix: A pull-through cache takes pulls for a configured upstream name, fetches the manifest and the layers from the upstream on the first request, stores them by digest, and answers later requests itself. Manifests fetched by a mutable tag are given a short freshness time so that the tag is checked again soon, while blobs are immutable and are kept as long as they are used. Concurrent requests for the same missing layer are collapsed into one upstream download. When the upstream is down the cache still serves what it holds.
steps.tradeoff: Deployments stop depending on someone else's availability and quota, and the bytes cross the internet once. The cache holds a copy of third-party content that nobody here reviewed, so it must be scanned like everything else, and a tag served from cache can be a little stale.

steps.title: Replicate to every region
steps.problem: Pulling a 500 MB image across an ocean for every node is slow and expensive, and a single region is a single point of failure for deployments.
steps.fix: Each region has its own blob store and metadata. When a manifest is pushed, a replication job copies the manifest and only the layers that the target region does not have, which is a digest comparison and not a copy of everything. The target verifies each digest as it stores. Because blobs are immutable and named by hash, replication can be retried freely and can never produce a half-changed layer. A region can also fetch a missing image on demand from its home region and then keep it, like a pull-through cache.
steps.tradeoff: Pulls stay inside the region and a regional outage does not stop the others. Storage and transfer costs are multiplied by the number of regions, and a tag may exist in the home region a few seconds or minutes before it exists elsewhere, so deployment tools should wait for the digest to arrive.

steps.title: Collect garbage without racing a push
steps.problem: Untagged images and orphan layers pile up and cost money, but a layer that nobody references yet may be the one that a push uploaded a minute ago and is about to reference.
steps.fix: Garbage collection has two phases. Mark walks every tag and every manifest and collects the set of digests that are still needed. Sweep deletes blobs that are not in that set. To avoid the race, a blob is never swept before it has reached a minimum age longer than the longest push plus one collection run, and any request that finds an existing blob, such as a HEAD during a push, refreshes its age. Manifest commits check that every named blob exists. For stricter safety the collector can take a short lease (a time-limited lock) on the repository and put it in read-only mode while it sweeps, or use a reference count in the metadata database that is updated in the same transaction as the manifest.
steps.tradeoff: Storage is reclaimed, and a push in progress is never robbed of its layers. Unreferenced data stays for the length of the grace period, a read-only window delays pushes, and a collector bug is the one bug in this system that destroys data, so it needs a dry-run mode (list what would be deleted, delete nothing) and a delay before the actual delete.

steps.title: Scan new images, sign them, and enforce it at deploy time
steps.problem: A digest proves the bytes did not change, but not who made them or whether they contain a library with a known critical flaw.
steps.fix: A push publishes an event and a scanner reads the layers, lists the packages inside, and compares them with a vulnerability database, storing the report against the image digest. The scan is repeated on a schedule, because new flaws are published for old images. The build pipeline signs the manifest digest with a key held in a key service, or with a short-lived identity from the pipeline, and the signature is stored next to the image as another small artifact that refers to the digest. A deployment gate in the cluster pulls the signature and the latest report and refuses an unsigned image or one with a critical finding.
steps.tradeoff: Only images built by the pipeline and not known to be dangerous reach production, and the same data answers 'where do we run the vulnerable library?'. Scanners produce false alarms and a gate that blocks deployments needs an emergency override and a clear owner. Key management is a new thing that must be protected and rotated.

failures.scenario: The garbage collector sweeps a layer while a push is committing
failures.impact: A manifest ends up pointing at a layer that no longer exists, and every pull of that image fails.
failures.answer: Layers younger than a grace period are never swept, a HEAD hit refreshes a layer's age, and the manifest commit verifies that all layers exist. Sweeping can run against a snapshot, with a delay between choosing and deleting, so that a mistake can be undone. If an image is found broken anyway, the build is rerun to upload the missing layer, since the manifest names its digest exactly.

failures.scenario: A deploy pulls a tag that was moved to a different image
failures.impact: Half of the servers run the old version and half the new one, and nobody can tell which is which.
failures.answer: Deployment configuration records the digest that a tag resolved to, and servers pull by digest. Release tags can be made immutable so that pushing the same tag again is refused. The 'latest' tag is allowed to move, but nothing in production depends on it.

failures.scenario: A region has a tag but not yet all of its layers
failures.impact: A node pulls the manifest and fails on the first layer that has not arrived.
failures.answer: A region publishes the tag only after the manifest and every layer have been stored and verified, so the tag appears all at once. Deployment tools that wait for a digest poll for it, and a pull for a missing image falls back to fetching it from the home region.

failures.scenario: The public registry rate-limits or goes down during a big deploy
failures.impact: Thousands of nodes get errors for a base image they need, and the rollout stalls.
failures.answer: Nodes pull from the pull-through cache, which holds the layers already fetched and collapses concurrent requests for a missing one into a single upstream download. A circuit breaker stops the cache from hammering a failing upstream, and important base images are pre-fetched ahead of time.

failures.scenario: A critical vulnerability is published for a library inside images already running
failures.impact: Hundreds of images in production were clean when they passed the scan and are now not.
failures.answer: The scanner re-checks stored images against the updated database and attaches new findings to the digest. An alert lists the affected digests and the services running them, the deployment gate blocks new rollouts of them, and the fix is a rebuilt image with a new digest rather than a change to the old one.

alternatives.title: Where the blobs are stored

options.name: A local disk on each registry server
options.pro: Simple and fast for a small team
options.con: Capacity and durability are tied to one machine, and servers cannot share it

options.name: An object store, served by redirect
options.pro: Durable, nearly unlimited, and downloads bypass the API servers
options.con: Each request has more latency, and listing and deleting need care

options.name: An object store with a disk cache in front
options.pro: Hot layers are served locally while the object store keeps everything
options.con: Another layer to size and keep consistent

alternatives.pick: An object store with redirects to a CDN. Add a local cache only for hot, small layers.

alternatives.title: Tags that move, or tags that cannot

options.name: Mutable tags
options.con: The same name can mean different images on different days

options.name: Immutable tags
options.pro: A version name always means the same image
options.con: A mistaken release needs a new tag, and cleanup rules must account for it

options.name: Pull by digest only
options.con: Unreadable, so tools must translate a tag to a digest at release time

alternatives.pick: Immutable release tags, mutable development tags, and deployments that pin the digest.

alternatives.title: How to collect garbage safely

options.name: Stop the world: read-only mode while collecting
options.con: Pushes are blocked, for longer as the registry grows

options.name: Online mark and sweep with a grace period
options.pro: No downtime, and the rule is easy to state
options.con: Garbage lives a little longer, and the grace must exceed the longest push plus a run

options.name: Reference counts updated with each manifest
options.pro: A blob is deleted the moment it is unreferenced
options.con: Counts can drift after bugs, so a periodic mark and sweep is still needed

alternatives.pick: Online mark and sweep with a grace period, run in dry-run mode first, with read-only mode as an emergency option.

alternatives.title: How to fill other regions

options.name: Push everything to every region
options.pro: Every image is local, so pulls are always fast
options.con: Pays for storage and transfer of images that a region never runs

options.name: Pull on demand from the home region
options.pro: Only what is used is copied
options.con: The first pull in a region is slow, and a home region outage hurts

options.name: Replicate chosen repositories, and pull the rest on demand
options.pro: Production images are ready ahead of time and the long tail costs little
options.con: Someone must decide which repositories count as production

alternatives.pick: Replicate production repositories eagerly and everything else on demand.

alternatives.title: How to sign images

options.name: Long-lived keys held by the pipeline
options.con: A stolen key signs anything until it is found and rotated

options.name: Short-lived keys tied to the pipeline's identity
options.pro: Nothing long-lived to steal, and the signature says which pipeline built it
options.con: Needs an identity provider and a log of issued certificates

alternatives.pick: Short-lived signing identities, with the gate checking which pipeline and repository produced the image.

roles.label: Clients
roles.description: Builds that push, servers that pull, and the public registry upstream.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The registry API, the CDN and the pull-through cache.

roles.label: Uploads
roles.description: Upload sessions that receive chunks and can be resumed.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The blob store, the tag and manifest database, and the regional copies.

quiz.question: A build server pushes a 2 GB layer in a single HTTP request over a flaky link. About a third of the pushes break near the end and start again from zero. What should the registry offer?
options: Upload sessions that take chunks at explicit offsets, report progress after a failure, and check the final digest
Automatic retry of the whole request up to three times with exponential backoff and jitter, giving each push four chances to succeed
Gzip compression of the layer in transit, so that the request is much shorter and fewer connections are dropped on the way
A larger timeout on the load balancer, so that a slow upload is not cut off while the client is still sending data
quiz.explanation: With offsets the client asks where the upload stands and sends only the rest, and the digest check at the end proves the bytes. Retrying the whole request repeats the same loss, and compression or a longer timeout do not address breaks in the connection.

quiz.question: A critical flaw is published in a library that sits in a base layer used by about 400 images running in production. All 400 passed the registry's scan when they were pushed last month. What should the registry do?
options: Do nothing until each team pushes a new build, because a scan result describes the image at the moment of the push and the teams own the fixes
Re-scan stored images against the new database, flag each digest, block new rollouts of them, and require rebuilt images
Rewrite the affected layer in place with the patched library and keep the same digest, so that no manifest or deployment needs to change at all
Delete every tag that points at an affected image, so that no node can pull a vulnerable version again after a restart or scale-up
quiz.explanation: New flaws are published after images are built, so scans must be repeated, and the result is tied to the digest. A digest names exact bytes, so a fix is a new image with a new digest. Deleting tags would break nodes that restart and still would not tell anyone where the library runs.

quiz.question: A registry runs garbage collection every hour, deleting blobs that no manifest references. Large pushes over a slow VPN take up to 40 minutes, and layers are uploaded before the manifest that refers to them. Collection skips blobs younger than 30 minutes. Which fix lets collection run without blocking pushes?
options: Shorten the collection interval to 10 minutes, so that each run has less unreferenced data to examine and finishes sooner
Put the registry in read-only mode for the duration of every collection run, then switch pushes back on
Count references in a nightly batch job and delete blobs that have a count of zero at that moment
Set the minimum age above 100 minutes (longest push plus one run), and refresh a blob's age when a push finds it with HEAD
quiz.explanation: A layer can wait unreferenced for the whole push, so it must survive at least that long plus the gap before the next run. A shorter interval does not change that race, and a nightly count can delete a layer of a push that has not committed yet. Read-only mode would block pushes.
